name: SIMDNoise (simdnoise crate)
baseline: the crate's own scalar (non-SIMD) fallback implementation of the same noise generators
workload: Time to generate one 2D 4k (3840 x 2160) Fbm noise block with 3 octaves, and one 3D 128 x 128 x 128 cell noise block, single-threaded, measured with Criterion.rs.
claimed_speedup: 2D 4k Fbm 3 octaves: scalar 888 ms, sse2 225 ms, sse41 186 ms, avx2 108 ms (avx2 about 8.2x vs scalar, derived from page data). 3D 128^3 cell noise: scalar 1,400 ms, sse2 128 ms, sse41 94 ms, avx2 47 ms (avx2 about 29.8x vs scalar, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (README names Criterion.rs only; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS are absent). Benchmark source is benches/benchmarks.rs in the repo.
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not directly callable from C++ without an FFI wrapper. x86 only (SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2 plus FMA3, runtime detection picks the best set); README lists AVX-512 and ARM NEON as TODO. Output is noise generation only, not a general SIMD wrapper.
caveats: Baseline is the crate's own scalar fallback, not a third-party library, so the claim shows the benefit of SIMD for this algorithm rather than a win over an independent incumbent. The README table is undated and the last commit (2024-11-20) was 'port benchmarks to simdeez v2', so the numbers may predate the current code. Compiler version and flags are not stated, which keeps the tier at C. i7-6700 is a 2015 CPU. Repo is the maintained continuation (current maintainer Peter Reijnders) of Jack Mott's original; Cargo.toml gives license as 'Apache-2.0/MIT'. The HN thread was seen only as a search-result title; its comments were not readable.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com with query 'Show HN SIMD library AVX2 NEON faster than benchmark github C' returned the thread 'Show HN: A SIMD-accelerated noise library in Rust' (item 17333044); repo and README opened on github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Vector Class Library (VCL) version 2
baseline: standard scalar math function libraries (libm) and scalar code that the compiler fails to auto-vectorize
workload: No benchmark workload is published. The manual states qualitatively that vector math functions (log, exp, pow, trig, hyperbolic) process whole SIMD vectors and so beat scalar math libraries, and that VCL gives the same optimization level as hand-written intrinsics.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. Manual: 'Both versions are many times faster than standard (scalar) math function libraries' (inline and external SVML-based vector math versions).
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; used as a dependency by other libraries (for example andyD123/DR3 vendors a VCL2 copy)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only (SSE2 up to AVX-512 and AVX512-FP16 types); the README says there are no plans for ARM or other instruction sets. Header-only, C++17 or later. The external vector math library variant needs Intel's SVML (Intel compiler); the inline variant is portable across GCC, Clang and MSVC. Manual rates exp-type math functions as 'poor' efficiency relative to simple operations, though still faster than scalar alternatives.
caveats: Tier D: the speed claims have no benchmark, hardware, compiler or flags. Included under the single notable-D allowance (over 1k stars, very widely referenced, named repeatedly in HN threads about SIMD wrappers). The manual itself recommends compiler auto-vectorization where it works and positions VCL as the alternative when it fails. Manual date 2026-09-09 matches the latest commit.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com for SIMD wrapper libraries surfaced the threads 'It's much better to use any of the numerous SIMD wrappers such as libsimdpp or V...' (item 11418471) and 'Design of a low-level C++ template SIMD library [pdf]' (item 16050021); the HN thread text was not readable, the project was identified from the truncated title and opened on github.com. The manual PDF was fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com and read with pdftotext.

name: intel-intrinsics (inteli, SIMD library for D)
baseline: Phobos std.digest.sha sha256Of (scalar D standard-library SHA-256)
workload: SHA-256 of a 1,024,000-byte buffer (512 * 2000 bytes of 'a'), repeated 1000 times, comparing std.digest.sha sha256Of against a SHA-NI implementation written with inteli intrinsics (examples/sha256/source/main.d); both print elapsed microseconds and the digest.
claimed_speedup: README: '18x faster SHA-256 vs Phobos' with intel-intrinsics; separately cites a 3.5x speed-up for some particular loops in a DConf 2019 talk and dg2d renderer 'twice as fast as Cairo' (unmeasured on the page).
compiler_and_flags: LDC; example dub.json sets dflags-ldc ["-mattr=+sha,+sse4.2,+popcnt"]; LDC version and optimisation level not stated.
stars_or_usage: 73 stars; used by Auburn Sounds and Cut Through Recordings audio products, dg2d and PixelPerfectEngine
tradeoffs: D language only (usable from C++ only by calling D code through a C ABI). Provides the Intel intrinsics API (MMX to AVX2, F16C, BMI2) with one syntax across LDC, DMD and GDC and emulates it on AArch64 and 32-bit ARM. Project states semantics are preserved even at the cost of speed. SHA-NI benchmark needs a CPU with SHA extensions. ARM differences: MXCSR emulated through FPCR, masked loads and stores need padded buffers.
caveats: The 18x figure is a README claim without hardware or timing output; the benchmark source prints times but the repo does not record results. Baseline is Phobos' portable D SHA-256, not an optimised library such as OpenSSL, and the fast path relies on dedicated SHA-NI instructions rather than generic SIMD, so the ratio reflects hardware offload as much as the library. Example code is derived from the Crypto++ SHA-SIMD reference (Walton, Blumenthal, Raad) by Johan Engelen (public domain). Claims for dg2d versus Cairo and the 3.5x talk figure have no numbers on the page and are not part of this entry's tier.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com for 'portable SIMD library AVX2 NEON' returned the SIMDe/SIMD Everywhere threads (items 24048562, 37706070) where the README of intel-intrinsics names SIMDe as its closest relative; project found on github.com/topics/simd-intrinsics, README and example opened.
